A phase carried by black-hole flow

29 July 2026 · based on arXiv:2605.28582

A classical flow tells us how density moves. A quantum amplitude must also remember phase. Around a black hole, that additional bookkeeping produces a geometric effect with an Aharonov–Bohm character.

The starting point is deliberately concrete. Choose a geodesic velocity field on a Schwarzschild background and evolve a density along it. The continuity equation then tracks compression, dilution, and horizon crossing. This is already useful geometry: it turns a congruence of trajectories into a flow of matter. But a density cannot interfere. To ask a quantum question, the transported object must be a complex amplitude.

From density to amplitude

The amplitude equation contains the same transport responsible for the density, together with a phase evolution inherited from the curved background and the chosen angular mode. In the reduced system the phase is not an arbitrary decoration placed on top of the flow. It is an integral of the angular component of the velocity along the trajectory. For a mode with angular number k, the contribution is correspondingly k-dependent.

This is why the effect is naturally compared with the Aharonov–Bohm phenomenon. The local transport can be described along each path, while the accumulated relative phase records global geometric information. The comparison is structural rather than identical: here the geometry of black-hole flow, not a confined electromagnetic flux tube, supplies the phase.

The horizon is part of the calculation

Schwarzschild coordinates are poorly suited to deciding whether a transported quantity genuinely crosses the horizon. The flow was therefore checked in Kruskal–Szekeres variables, where the horizon is regular. The density and phase diagnostics can then be followed through the crossing rather than terminated at a coordinate singularity. Numerical notebooks matter here because they expose the behaviour directly and make the analytic reduction reproducible.

The broader lesson is that quantum geometry need not begin with a vague claim that spacetime is “nonclassical.” It can begin with a more disciplined question: given a concrete geometric flow, what happens when density is upgraded to amplitude, and which phase information survives? That question produces an observable-style output while remaining close to the underlying geometry.
